name: British Empire
borderNames: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
summary: The largest empire in history, ruling about a quarter of the world’s people and land at its height around 1920. It began with English and Scottish overseas ventures in the 16th–17th centuries; this entry covers its peak era from 1801 to the 1997 Hong Kong handover.

knownFor.label: Royal Navy
knownFor.note: The world’s largest navy for about two centuries.

knownFor.label: Steam engine & railways
knownFor.note: Industrial Revolution technology spread across the empire.

knownFor.label: Tea & cotton trade
knownFor.note: Tea from India and China; cotton cloth from Lancashire.

location.value: Ruled from London over territories on every inhabited continent. At its height it covered 24% of the Earth’s land: “the empire on which the sun never sets”.

terrain.value: An island base with a dominant navy, linked to colonies by sea lanes and strategic ports (Gibraltar, Suez, Aden, Singapore, Hong Kong).

climate.value: Ranged from temperate settler colonies (Canada, Australia, New Zealand) to tropical colonies in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean.

resources.value: Industrial Britain drew on cotton, sugar, tea, rubber, tin, gold and other colonial products, and on large markets for its manufactured goods.

disasters.value: Severe famines occurred under British rule in India (e.g. 1876–78, Bengal 1943) and in Ireland (1845–52). Historians debate how much colonial policy contributed to them.

population.value: 412 million people in 1913, 23% of the world’s population at the time (Wikipedia).

urbanisation.value: London was the world’s largest city in the 19th century. Colonial port cities such as Bombay, Calcutta, Singapore and Hong Kong grew rapidly.

disease.value: Epidemics in colonies (cholera, plague in India, the 1918 influenza) caused huge death tolls.

migration.value: Millions of British settlers emigrated to settler colonies. Over three million enslaved Africans were transported in British ships before abolition. Indian and Chinese indentured labourers moved across the empire.

economicBase.value: Trade, finance, shipping and industrial manufacturing, powered by the Industrial Revolution, with colonies supplying raw materials and markets.

tradeRoutes.value: Global sea lanes. The East India Company’s trade with India and China (including opium). Atlantic trade (sugar and, until 1807, the slave trade). After 1846, a free-trade empire.

wealth.value: Britain was the world’s richest major economy per person for much of the 19th century. Colonies varied hugely, and many remained poor.

moneyAndTax.value: The pound sterling and the gold standard underpinned world finance. Colonial taxes funded colonial administrations.

inequality.value: Deep inequality between colonisers and colonised, and racial hierarchies within colonies. Self-governing white settler dominions had far more rights than other colonies.

governmentType.value: Ruled by the British Crown and Parliament, which was the supreme law-making authority. The territories had many different statuses: dominions, crown colonies, protectorates, mandates and the Indian Raj.

keyRulers.value: Monarchs from George III to Elizabeth II, with prime ministers such as Pitt, Palmerston, Disraeli, Gladstone and Churchill. The East India Company ruled much of India until 1858.

succession.value: A hereditary constitutional monarchy, with power held by Parliament and elected governments in Britain.

institutions.value: Parliament, common law, the civil service (including the Indian Civil Service), colonial governors, and, after 1931, the Commonwealth.

stability.value: Lost the Thirteen American Colonies (1776–1783). Faced the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the Irish independence struggle (1919–21), and anti-colonial movements after 1945 (e.g. India, Kenya, Malaya).

eliteConflict.value: Political debate in Britain between expansionists and critics, and over Irish Home Rule, free trade and imperial preference.

armyAndTech.value: The Royal Navy was the world’s dominant navy after 1815 (“Pax Britannica”). Armies were raised largely from colonies, especially the British Indian Army.

majorWars.value: The Seven Years’ War (1756–63), the Battle of Plassey (1757), the Napoleonic Wars (to 1815), the Opium Wars, the Boer War (1899–1902), and both World Wars.

territoryChange.value: Largest extent after the First World War: 35.5 million km² in 1920 (24% of the world’s land).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Netherlands, France (until 1815), Russia (“the Great Game”) and Germany. Allies: Japan (1902), France and Russia (1904–07), and the US in the World Wars.

inventions.value: The Industrial Revolution (steam power, railways, the telegraph) originated in Britain and was spread across the empire with railways, telegraph cables and steamships.

scienceEducation.value: Universities and English-medium schools were established in colonies. Colonial education reached a minority but created new educated elites, many of whom led independence movements.

openness.value: Free-trade policy after 1846, and global flows of capital and people. Rule was often authoritarian and racially exclusive.

religion.value: Protestant Christianity (the Church of England) in Britain, and missionary activity across the empire. It ruled many Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist and other societies.

languageWriting.value: English, which spread worldwide as a result of the empire and remains a global language. Its legal and cultural legacy is widespread.

artsArchitecture.value: Colonial architecture (e.g. in Mumbai, Kuala Lumpur, Singapore), Victorian literature, and the spread of sports such as cricket and football.

socialStructure.value: Class-divided Britain, and racial hierarchies in colonies. Slavery was abolished across most of the empire by the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, after the slave trade was banned in 1807.

sharedIdentity.value: A sense of “Britishness” among settlers. Colonised peoples often developed national identities in opposition to empire.

neighbours.value: A global empire with neighbours on every continent: France, Russia, the Ottomans, Qing China, the US and others.

ideasReligions.value: Spread English, parliamentary government, common law, sport and Christianity. It also spread nationalist and anti-colonial ideas that later ended the empire.

colonisation.value: The largest colonial empire in history. Its rule brought railways and institutions but also conquest, violence, famine and economic exploitation, and its legacy remains debated.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: British Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026); Darwin, The Empire Project (2009)

riseSignals.value: Naval power, commercial companies (the East India Company), victories over the Netherlands and France in the 17th–18th centuries, and the Industrial Revolution.

peakPeriod.value: The 19th and early 20th centuries, when it was the foremost global power. Largest extent around 1920.

declineSignals.value: The cost of two World Wars, the rise of the US and USSR, nationalist movements, economic weakness, and the Suez Crisis (1956), which exposed British limits.

outcome.value: Decolonisation. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, then most of Africa, Asia and the Caribbean by the 1960s–80s. The handover of Hong Kong (1997) is often seen as the symbolic end. Most former colonies joined the Commonwealth.

sources.value: Government and colonial archives, parliamentary records, and colonial and anti-colonial writings. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (later sections only summarised). See also Darwin (2009).

overallCertainty.value: High for dates, territory and population. Interpretations of the empire’s legacy, especially famines, violence and economic effects, are strongly debated. Second source: Wikidata starts in 1583 (first colonies); this app’s entry starts in 1801, with Great Britain (1707–1800) as a separate entry.
